54_threshold_theorem.notes: Authored per the M4 standard. All three registered objectives covered: state the threshold theorem and its assumptions; explain why arbitrarily long computation becomes possible below threshold; distinguish fault-tolerant from merely error-detecting constructions. The theorem is stated with both load-bearing clauses emphasised (below a certain rate; polylogarithmic overhead), and seven assumptions are listed explicitly - local noise, Markovian noise, parallel gates, fresh resettable ancillas, fast correct classical decoding, no leakage, known noise strength - with the point made that real hardware violates several. Fault tolerance defined operationally as a property of the CIRCUIT not the code: any single fault anywhere must leave at most t errors per output block. FT gadget verified: transversal CNOT between two Steane blocks, CNOT(A_i,B_i) for i=0..6, verified to implement logical CNOT with A as control (X_L=XXXIIII, Z_L=ZZZIIII, both in N(S) not in S, anticommuting; the four conjugation images are exactly logical CNOT). FT property verified: each physical CNOT touches one qubit per block so one fault gives at most one error per block, and all 21 weight-1 errors on a Steane block are correctable - therefore P_fail = O(p^2). Non-FT gadget verified: bare ancilla on the weight-4 X-stabiliser IIIXXXX, an X fault on the ancilla control after k of 4 CNOTs induces a weight (4-k) data error. Exhaustively verified result: k=0 weight 4 is HARMLESS (it is the stabiliser itself, acts trivially); k=1 weight 3 is correctable by DEGENERACY (X on {4,5,6} differs from X on {3} by the stabiliser); k=2 weight 2 is NOT correctable (recovery finds X on {0} with the same syndrome but the product is not a stabiliser); k=3 weight 1 correctable. So one fault defeats the code and P_fail = O(p). The p vs p^2 separation table verified. Fixes listed: verified cat states (Shor), Steane ancillas, flag qubits, repeat-and-decode-in-space-time. Arbitrarily-long-computation result verified: union bound gives p_L <= eps/T, inverted to d ~ log T, overhead ~ (log T)^2; table at p_th=1e-2, A=0.1, p=1e-3, eps=1e-2 gives d=7,13,19,25,31,41 for T=1e3..1e20, i.e. 49 to 1681 qubits - a 10^17 longer computation costs 34x the qubits. Threshold magnitudes quoted as order-of-magnitude with the explicit caveat that they are a joint property of code, decoder and noise model (code capacity ~10%, phenomenological ~3%, circuit-level ~0.5-1%). Eastin-Knill stated as the price, with magic-state distillation as the workaround and the explicit warning that the qubit counts in this lesson are a floor not an estimate. 189/189 KaTeX compile. 23 RAG chunks, 0 unbalanced fences, max 1804.

63_complexity_classes.notes: Authored per the M4 standard against the registered spec (title 'BQP, P, NP and BPP', topic hw.complexity_classes, prereq algo.grover recommended). All three registered objectives covered: define BQP, BPP and NP; state the known inclusions relating these classes; explain what quantum speed-up evidence does and does not establish. The principal value of this lesson is negative - distinguishing proven theorems from conjecture - so the content is organised explicitly around that split. (1) Definitions: P, BPP (bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time, error at most 1/3), NP (certificate verifiable in polynomial time), BQP (polynomial-size quantum circuit, polynomial time, error at most 1/3, gates specified to polynomial precision). Two commonly-missed features are drawn out: the bounded-error condition is part of the definition and is amplifiable at polynomial cost, and the polynomial-precision gate requirement is needed to keep the class physical. (2) Known inclusions stated as theorems, not conjectures: P subset BPP subset BQP subset PP subset PSPACE, each with its provenance given (BQP subset PP is Adleman-DeMarrais-Huang), plus the tighter BQP subset AWPP and BQP subset P^#P, and NP subset PP. (3) Unknowns stated plainly: whether any inclusion is strict, whether BQP exceeds BPP, whether NP is in BQP (believed no) or BQP in NP (believed no), with the classes described as believed incomparable in the middle. The key structural point is included: proving BQP != BPP would immediately prove P != PSPACE, which is why the question is so hard. (4) Oracle separations (Simon, Bernstein-Vazirani, Raz-Tal 2018 BQP not subset PH) are correctly characterised as evidence about PROOF TECHNIQUES rather than proofs about the unrelativised world, and the strongest real-world evidence is identified as Shor (factoring in BQP, not known to be in P). (5) Objective 3 is the centrepiece: what sampling experiments do and do not establish. The exponential-state-space explanation is verified numerically - 2^n amplitudes at 16 bytes each gives 16.8 MB at n=20, 17.2 GB at n=30, 17.6 TB at n=40, 18.0 PB at n=50, 18.5 EB at n=60, and 1.27e30 amplitudes at n=100 - and the lesson states that this is the honest content of a sampling speed-up claim. Four things it does NOT establish are listed: it does not prove BQP != BPP (the sampling tasks are not decision problems in BQP and the hardness rests on unproven assumptions), it does not show the device does anything useful, it does not show a speed-up over the best classical algorithm for a useful problem, and it says nothing about NP-complete problems. items.lesson_title: Error Mitigation: ZNE, PEC and Readout Correction
items.review_notes: Authored per the M4 standard. All three registered objectives covered: explain the difference between error mitigation and error correction; apply zero-noise extrapolation to a noisy expectation value; construct and apply a readout error correction matrix. Core distinction stated up front with a 7-row comparison table: correction returns a corrected QUANTUM STATE, mitigation returns a corrected EXPECTATION VALUE (classical number) and therefore cannot be applied mid-circuit or scaled arbitrarily. ZNE verified by execution on a 2-qubit circuit (2 RY, 1 RX, 2 CX) against O = 1.0 ZI + 0.6 IZ + 0.4 ZZ with 1% depolarising on single-qubit gates and 3% on CX, using exact density-matrix expectation values so the improvement is pure bias correction: ideal 1.085661, raw 1.011469 (err -0.074192), ZNE linear 1.078276 (10.05x), quadratic 1.084856 (92.15x), cubic 1.085571 (817x), exponential 1.085719 (1289x). Underlying noisy values decay 1.011469 (lambda=1) to 0.660987 (lambda=7). Silent failure mode documented and hit in practice: folding then transpiling lets the optimiser cancel C^dagger C, removing the noise scaling entirely - transpile first, then fold. Variance cost verified: sum of squared Lagrange coefficients is 2.50 (linear) and 5.22 (quadratic), i.e. 1.58x and 2.28x the standard error. PEC verified: coefficients derived in the Pauli transfer matrix basis, a_I = 1 + 3p/(4(1-p)), a_P = -p/(4(1-p)), gamma = 1 + 3p/(2(1-p)); verified numerically that Lambda^-1 Lambda = I to machine precision for p=0.01,0.05,0.10. Monte Carlo with 2 million shot-level samples at p=0.05: bias removed from -0.032011 to -0.000004 and variance ratio 1.192 against the theoretical (gamma^2 - <O>^2)/(1 - <O>_noisy^2) = 1.194. Exponential cost verified: gamma^(2N) at p=0.01 is 1.16 (N=10), 4.50 (N=100), 3.40e6 (N=1000). Readout correction verified on 2 qubits with P(1|0)=0.03, P(0|1)=0.05, 40000 shots per calibration circuit: columns sum to 1, tensor-product prediction matches the full calibrated matrix to 0.0017 (shot noise), Bell-state total variation distance from ideal cut from 0.0767 to 0.00087 (88x improvement). The expected failure mode is reported honestly: the corrected 01 entry came out NEGATIVE at -0.0009 because M^-1 is not a stochastic map. Calibration cost table verified: 2^n circuits and 4^n matrix entries, 1.05e6 circuits at 20 qubits. 192/192 KaTeX compile. 23 RAG chunks, 0 unbalanced fences, max 1741.

All three registered objectives covered: describe how a transmon encodes a qubit; state typical coherence times and gate fidelities; identify the dominant error mechanisms. Physics verified by direct numerical diagonalisation of the transmon Hamiltonian H = 4 E_C (n - n_g)^2 - E_J cos(phi) in the charge basis (|n| <= 25), not quoted from memory. Three results verified at E_C/h = 250 MHz across E_J/E_C = 1, 5, 20, 50, 100: (1) the anharmonicity alpha = w12 - w01 converges to -E_C (numerical -0.2739 GHz vs -E_C = -0.2500 GHz at ratio 100); (2) the transition frequency follows sqrt(8 E_J E_C) - E_C (numerical 4.7355 vs analytic 4.7500 GHz at ratio 50, and 6.8113 vs 6.8211 at ratio 100), landing at ~4.7 GHz which is inside the real 4-6 GHz band; (3) the charge dispersion collapses by EIGHT orders of magnitude, from 7.8e-01 GHz at ratio 1 to 6.3e-09 GHz at ratio 100 - this is the whole point of the transmon and it is computed, not asserted. Device parameters (T1 100-300 us, T2 100-350 us, 1q error 1e-4 to 1e-3, 2q error 1e-3 to 1e-2, 2q gate 25-300 ns, readout error 5e-3 to 2e-2) taken from published 2024-2026 sources including a 2025 EPJ Quantum Technology review (IBM medians T1=288us, T2=127us, mean 1q EPG 6.75e-4, mean 2q EPG 1.15e-2), Toshiba/RIKEN 2024 (T1=230us, 99.90% 2q over 12 hours), Aalto 2025 (T1 median 425us, max 666us), and Google Willow (1.1 us surface-code cycle). The 17x gap between one-qubit and two-qubit error is highlighted as the platform's defining characteristic. Coherence-limited error floor verified by execution: epsilon ~ t_g/3T1 + t_g/3T2 across four parameter sets gives a depth budget T2/t_g of only 600 to 1200 two-qubit gates, and the best achieved 2q errors (~1e-3) are within a factor of 2-3 of that floor, so coherence rather than control is the binding constraint. (1) Single-qubit gates are DETERMINISTIC: built the exact bosonic Fock-space operator U_Fock = exp(sum_ij (log U)_ij a_i^dag a_j) for a two-mode beam splitter and verified that leakage from the one-photon subspace is 0 to numerical precision (0.0e+00 to 4.4e-16) at reflectivity R = 0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, and that the induced 2x2 matrix on the dual-rail qubit is unitary at every R. At R = 1 it gives i sigma_x. This is the reason single-qubit gates need no post-selection, and it is stated as the contrast with two-qubit gates. (2) Hong-Ou-Mandel interference verified over the full Fock space: the |1,1> output amplitude is t^2 - r^2 = 1 - 2R, confirmed against the closed form (1-2R)^2 at R = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 with exact agreement. items.lesson_title: Calibrated Noise Models and Connectivity Topologies
items.review_notes: Authored per the M4 standard against the registered spec (title 'Calibrated Noise Models and Connectivity Topologies', topic hw.platform_comparison, prereqs hw.superconducting_qubits REQUIRED and hw.trapped_ions recommended - both now satisfied). All three registered objectives covered: read a calibrated noise model for a device; compare connectivity topologies across platforms; choose a platform appropriate to a given workload. This lesson MEANINGFULLY COMPARES rather than listing, per the standing directive. (1) Reading a calibrated noise model: the real calibration snapshot shipped with a 127-qubit superconducting device extracted and tabulated - median T1 279.6 us (range 40.9-458.8), T2 197.8 us (16.9-423.3), readout error 1.17% (best 0.33%, worst 35.75%), two-qubit gate error 0.80% (best 0.36%, worst 7.40%), single-qubit 0.021%, two-qubit duration 533 ns, single-qubit 57 ns, qubit frequency median 4.79 GHz. Four non-obvious readings are drawn out rather than just the headline fidelity: the T2/T1 ratio is 0.752 not 2, so the qubit is strongly DEPHASING-limited and T2 is actually shorter than T1; the native two-qubit gate is ECR not CNOT, so a logical CNOT costs more than the quoted figure; single-qubit gates are 250x better and 9x faster than two-qubit, which should drive compilation; and the worst qubit is 10x worse than the median, making qubit selection a real optimisation. (2) Connectivity: the same device has 144 edges against 8001 for all-to-all, i.e. 1.80% of all-to-all edges, mean degree 2.27, max degree 3 (heavy-hex), diameter 26, mean shortest path 11.13. (3) The cost of sparse connectivity measured by COMPILING, not estimating: a QFT transpiled onto all-to-all, grid, ring and line at n = 9, 16, 25 with identical optimisation level and seed. Two-qubit gate counts 72/123/171/165, 240/462/645/588, 600/1191/1494/1485; depths 61/165/163/162, 117/417/428/358, 189/694/601/591. Ratios versus all-to-all: gate count line 2.29x/2.45x/2.48x and depth line 2.66x/3.06x/3.13x, with depth identified as the metric that matters since errors accumulate with depth. A genuinely useful negative result is reported: the naive SWAP estimate (mean path (n+1)/3 hops times 3 CNOTs, i.e. 10 CNOTs at n=9 and 26 at n=25) over-predicts by an order of magnitude, because real transpilers reorder operations and amortise a SWAP across several gates. This corrects the naive claim and is stated as such. (4) Choosing a platform is structured as 'which resource binds' - depth, connectivity, qubit count, fidelity, or manufacturability - with a worked variational-algorithm example whose answer depends on whether the ansatz can be restructured for the hardware. Both executable blocks run clean under -W error::Warning with only declared dependencies (qiskit + qiskit-aer); qiskit_ibm_runtime was used ONLY for offline extraction of the calibration table and deliberately kept out of the lesson because it is not a declared dependency. 142/142 KaTeX compile. 18 RAG chunks, 0 unbalanced fences, max 1821. Validator 59/59.

Authored per the M4 standard against the registered spec (title 'NISQ Limitations', topic hw.nisq_limitations, prereqs qiskit.quantum_noise required and adv.resource_estimation recommended). All three registered objectives covered: state the constraints defining the NISQ regime; explain why circuit depth is limited by error rates; assess whether a proposed algorithm fits current hardware. The central result is that the whole NISQ constraint reduces to one product N*d*eps, with P_success ~ (1-eps)^(N d) ~ exp(-N d eps) and usable depth d_max ~ ln2/(N eps). VERIFIED by simulation with the AerSimulator density_matrix method: random circuits on N=4 with depolarising eps=0.002 per CX give fidelity 0.995172, 0.989932, 0.979308, 0.959363, 0.939347, 0.919872, 0.881859, 0.845716 at depths 1,2,4,8,12,16,24,32 against predictions 0.994012, 0.988060, 0.976262, 0.953088, 0.930464, 0.908377, 0.865763, 0.825148; and on N=6 with eps=0.005 give 0.979345, 0.957291, 0.914464, 0.833948, 0.760410, 0.693452 at depths 1,2,4,8,12,16. The measured fidelity tracks the independent-error prediction closely and runs slightly ABOVE it, which is explained in the lesson: a depolarising channel leaves the state completely untouched with probability 1-eps rather than perturbing it slightly. A notable early failure is documented and fixed in the lesson notes: the naive statevector method silently ignores the noise model and returns F=1.0 at every depth, and only method='density_matrix' applies it. The budget table at eps=0.01 shows d for P=1/2 falling 17.3, 8.7, 4.3, 2.2, 1.1, 0.5 at N=4,8,16,32,64,128 - at 128 qubits the usable depth is below one entangling layer, which is stated as the NISQ wall reached by scaling qubits without improving error rates. The inversion table gives total CX gates available as ln2/eps: 69 at 1e-2, 693 at 1e-3, 6931 at 1e-4, 69315 at 1e-5, with depth on 50 qubits 1.4, 13.9, 138.6, 1386. Assessment of algorithm fit is given as five explicit checks plus four worked verdicts (VQE 20q depth 12 feasible with mitigation; Grover over 2^50 infeasible by orders of magnitude; Shor RSA-2048 infeasible needing fault tolerance; QAOA 100q p=1 right at the edge at 0.8 while p=10 gives 8). Three independent constraints identified: error budget, coherence, and qubit count with connectivity. 99/99 KaTeX compile. 16 RAG chunks, 0 unbalanced fences, max 1708. Validator 60/60.

Authored per the M4 standard against the registered spec (title 'BQP, P, NP and BPP', topic hw.complexity_classes, prereq algo.grover recommended). All three registered objectives covered: define BQP, BPP and NP; state the known inclusions relating these classes; explain what quantum speed-up evidence does and does not establish. The principal value of this lesson is negative - distinguishing proven theorems from conjecture - so the content is organised explicitly around that split. (1) Definitions: P, BPP (bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time, error at most 1/3), NP (certificate verifiable in polynomial time), BQP (polynomial-size quantum circuit, polynomial time, error at most 1/3, gates specified to polynomial precision). Two commonly-missed features are drawn out: the bounded-error condition is part of the definition and is amplifiable at polynomial cost, and the polynomial-precision gate requirement is needed to keep the class physical. (2) Known inclusions stated as theorems, not conjectures: P subset BPP subset BQP subset PP subset PSPACE, each with its provenance given (BQP subset PP is Adleman-DeMarrais-Huang), plus the tighter BQP subset AWPP and BQP subset P^#P, and NP subset PP. (3) Unknowns stated plainly: whether any inclusion is strict, whether BQP exceeds BPP, whether NP is in BQP (believed no) or BQP in NP (believed no), with the classes described as believed incomparable in the middle. The key structural point is included: proving BQP != BPP would immediately prove P != PSPACE, which is why the question is so hard. (4) Oracle separations (Simon, Bernstein-Vazirani, Raz-Tal 2018 BQP not subset PH) are correctly characterised as evidence about PROOF TECHNIQUES rather than proofs about the unrelativised world, and the strongest real-world evidence is identified as Shor (factoring in BQP, not known to be in P). (5) Objective 3 is the centrepiece: what sampling experiments do and do not establish. The exponential-state-space explanation is verified numerically - 2^n amplitudes at 16 bytes each gives 16.8 MB at n=20, 17.2 GB at n=30, 17.6 TB at n=40, 18.0 PB at n=50, 18.5 EB at n=60, and 1.27e30 amplitudes at n=100 - and the lesson states that this is the honest content of a sampling speed-up claim. Four things it does NOT establish are listed: it does not prove BQP != BPP (the sampling tasks are not decision problems in BQP and the hardness rests on unproven assumptions), it does not show the device does anything useful, it does not show a speed-up over the best classical algorithm for a useful problem, and it says nothing about NP-complete problems. A three-part bar for a genuine quantum advantage demonstration is given. 67/67 KaTeX compile. 15 RAG chunks, 0 unbalanced fences, max 1875. Validator 61/61.

Authored per the M4 standard against the registered spec (title 'Quantum Benchmarking', topic hw.benchmarking, prereqs hw.nisq_limitations required and hw.platform_comparison recommended - both now satisfied). All three registered objectives covered: describe randomised benchmarking and what it measures; define quantum volume and its limitations; choose a benchmark appropriate to a claimed capability. The distinguishing feature is that RB is VALIDATED rather than merely described: the protocol is run against a known injected error rate and checked. (1) Randomised benchmarking verified by simulation: random Clifford sequences with depolarising noise injected at parameter lambda, survival probability fitted to F(m) = A p^m + 1/2^n, converted to EPC = (2^n-1)(1-p)/2^n. Injected lambda = 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02 give fitted p = 0.99800, 0.99500, 0.99000, 0.98000 and EPC = 0.001000, 0.002500, 0.005000, 0.010000, matching theory p = 1-lambda and EPC = lambda/2 with 0.00% relative error at every rate. The full nine-point decay curve at lambda=0.01 matches theory to five decimal places at every m from 0 to 320. This is stated as the reason RB is trustworthy: it has been checked against a known answer rather than merely fitted to a decay. (2) A genuine implementation bug is documented in the lesson notes: an earlier version applied the inversion before the forward sequence, producing a survival curve that collapsed to 0.5 immediately and an EPC of 0.259 against a true 0.005 - a 50x error that would have produced a lesson teaching the opposite of the truth. Fixed by simulating the real ordering (Clifford, noise, ..., invert). (3) What RB does NOT measure is given equal weight: SPAM is absorbed into A, twirling destroys the error mechanism so only the average survives, and correlated and non-Markovian errors are invisible. (4) Quantum volume defined as 2^d for the largest square circuit passing at heavy-output probability above 2/3 at 2 sigma, with the power-of-two scale tabulated so a difference of 5 in d reads as a factor of 32. Verified the per-gate error QV demands: roughly d^2/2 two-qubit gates and eps ~ 0.105/(d^2/2) gives 1.31e-2 at d=4, 3.28e-3 at d=8, 8.20e-4 at d=16, 2.05e-4 at d=32, 5.13e-5 at d=64. (5) Objective 3 is a benchmark-versus-blind-to table plus claim-by-claim guidance: gate quality to two-qubit RB on ALL pairs (not the best pair, since the calibration lesson showed the worst qubit was 10x the median); depth to QV or layer fidelity; applications to the application against the best classical algorithm; error correction to a logical-error versus code-distance curve where the SIGN of the slope is the result. 76/76 KaTeX compile. 21 RAG chunks, 0 unbalanced fences, max 1492.
